lead: Every diffusion calculation needs one number: the diffusivity D_AB, the constant in Fick's law that says how quickly A spreads through B. You cannot read it from a table for every pair, so engineers either measure it in a small cell or predict it from simpler properties. Measurement gives the truth for one pair; prediction gives a quick estimate before a pilot plant exists. The same number sizes absorbers, dryers and membrane units. This chapter shows the standard methods for gases and liquids, the units each one uses, and the order of magnitude to expect.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.3 for Fick's laws and Chapter 1.4 for the flux equations used to interpret a measurement; the ideal gas law from Chapter 1.1.

sections.h3: What D is and how big it is

blocks.text: The diffusivity D_AB is the proportionality constant in Fick's first law for A diffusing through B. Its SI unit is m²/s; older tables use cm²/s, and 1 cm²/s = 10⁻⁴ m²/s. For a binary gas pair the number is symmetric: D_AB = D_BA. The value depends on temperature and pressure. Gases diffuse fast, liquids slow, solids far slower; Chapter 1.7 covers solids.

The orders matter in design. A gas-phase value near 10⁻⁵ m²/s means a species crosses a millimetre in about a tenth of a second; a liquid-phase value near 10⁻⁹ m²/s takes about a thousand seconds for the same distance. That is why absorbers and extraction columns use stirring, packing or small droplets: the molecular value alone would need an impractically tall column. See Unit 2 for how flow adds eddy diffusion.
All measurements put the pair in a known geometry, hold temperature constant, and follow concentration with time. The integrated form of Fick's law turns the slope of a log plot into D.

Two-bulb (Winkelmann) method for gases. Two bulbs of volume V each are joined by a tube of length L and cross-section S. One bulb starts rich in A, the other poor. With equal volumes and equimolar counter-diffusion, the mole-fraction difference Δy falls exponentially:

blocks.where: Δy₀ is the initial mole-fraction difference; Δy is the difference at time t; S is the tube cross-section in m²; L is the tube length in m; V is each bulb volume in m³; t is time in s.

blocks.text: A plot of ln(Δy₀/Δy) against t is a straight line through the origin, and D_AB comes from its slope. The Stefan tube measures a gas pair by the fall of a liquid level; Chapter 1.5 gives the pseudo-steady treatment, and the slope of level against time gives D.

For liquids the diaphragm cell is standard. Two stirred compartments are separated by a porous glass diaphragm. The cell constant β is found once by calibrating with a pair of known D, such as dilute KCl in water. Then ln(Δc₀/Δc) = β D_AB t. A closed cell with a sensor or optical window follows concentration against time in a still sample; fit the same exponential decay form, ln(Δc₀/Δc) = k t (k is the fitted slope), and extract D once the cell's geometric constant is known. Taylor dispersion is a modern flow method: a pulse is injected into laminar flow in a capillary, and the spread of the pulse gives D. Only a few universities teach it in the first course.

Kinetic theory gives the Chapman–Enskog equation. It needs Lennard–Jones parameters σ (collision diameter) and ε/k_B (energy well depth) for each species, plus a collision integral Ω_D that depends on T. The result is right to a few per cent for non-polar gases. The formula is long, so most hand calculations use the Fuller–Schettler–Giddings correlation.

blocks.where: D_AB is in cm²/s; T is in K; P is in atm; M_A and M_B are molar masses in g/mol; Σv_A and Σv_B are diffusion volume increments (tabulated numbers, not molar volumes); Σv_A<sup>1/3</sup> means the cube root of the tabulated increment Σv_A; the cube roots of A and B are added, and that sum is squared in the denominator. The 0.5 exponent applies only to (1/M_A + 1/M_B).

blocks.text: Read the dependence, not just the formula. D rises as T<sup>1.75</sup> and falls as 1/P. Doubling pressure halves D at the same temperature. The correlation gives cm²/s only when P is in atm; if you feed kPa you get a value too small by the conversion factor. Convert to m²/s at the end by multiplying by 10⁻⁴.
Liquid diffusivities are harder because molecules touch. The Stokes–Einstein relation treats the solute as a sphere of radius r moving through a continuum of viscosity μ:

blocks.where: k_B = 1.381×10⁻²³ J/K is the Boltzmann constant; T is absolute temperature in K; μ is viscosity in Pa·s; r is the solute radius in m; D_AB is in m²/s.

blocks.text: The relation shows the key scaling: D ∝ T/μ. Warm a liquid and D rises; add a thickener and D falls. It is accurate for large spherical solutes in a solvent, less so for small molecules of similar size to the solvent.

Wilke–Chang is the common engineering correlation. It uses the solvent viscosity μ_B, an association factor φ (about 2.6 for water, 1.9 for methanol, 1.0 for non-polar solvents) and the solute molar volume at its normal boiling point V_A. Hayduk–Laudie is an alternative that uses μ_B and V_A without φ. Both return cm²/s when viscosity is in cP and volume in cm³/mol. For a first estimate, check the correlation output lies near 10⁻⁵ cm²/s, that is 10⁻⁹ m²/s. A value near 10⁻¹ cm²/s (10⁻⁵ m²/s) means a gas correlation slipped in.

figure.caption: The two measurement routes and the two prediction routes for D. Notice that each route is tied to a phase: gas methods on the left and liquid methods on the right.

spec.aria: A tree splits diffusivity into measurement and prediction, then into gas and liquid methods: two-bulb and diaphragm cell for measurement, Fuller and Wilke–Chang for prediction.

examples.question: Estimate the diffusivity of CO2 in air at 300 K and 1 atm with the Fuller correlation. Data: M of CO2 = 44 g/mol, M of air = 29 g/mol, diffusion volume increments Σv = 26.9 for CO2 and 20.1 for air.
steps: Write the correlation with P in atm: D_AB = 1.00×10⁻³ T<sup>1.75</sup> (1/M_A + 1/M_B)<sup>0.5</sup> / [P (Σv_A<sup>1/3</sup> + Σv_B<sup>1/3</sup>)²], with D in cm²/s.
Compute the mass term: 1/44 + 1/29 = 0.02273 + 0.03448 = 0.05721. Its square root is 0.2392.
Compute the cube roots: 26.9^1/3 = 3.00 and 20.1^1/3 = 2.72. Their sum is 5.72, and the square is 32.7.
Convert: 1 cm²/s = 10⁻⁴ m²/s, so D_AB = 0.1584 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.584×10⁻⁵ m²/s.
examples.answer: D_AB for CO2 in air at 300 K and 1 atm is about 0.158 cm²/s, that is 1.58×10⁻⁵ m²/s.
examples.check:
import math
T = 300.0
P = 1.0
M_CO2 = 44.0
M_air = 29.0
Sv_CO2 = 26.9
Sv_air = 20.1
mass_term = math.sqrt(1/M_CO2 + 1/M_air)
D_cm2_s = 1.00e-3 * T**1.75 * mass_term / (P * (Sv_CO2**(1/3) + Sv_air**(1/3))**2)
D_m2_s = D_cm2_s * 1e-4
print(f"{D_cm2_s:.4f}")
print(f"{D_m2_s:.3e}")

traps: Fuller's correlation wants P in atm and returns cm²/s. Put 101.3 kPa in place of 1 atm and your answer is about 101 times too small.
T must be in kelvin. Using 27 for 27°C in T<sup>1.75</sup> gives a meaningless number.
Σv is a diffusion volume increment from a table, not the molar volume. Do not use 22.4 L/mol.
D_AB = D_BA for a binary gas pair. Do not mix D (m²/s) with the mass transfer coefficient k_c (m/s) from Unit 2.
Stokes–Einstein says D ∝ T/μ, not μ/T. Check the direction: a thicker liquid slows diffusion.

quiz.q: Define diffusivity D_AB and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: D_AB is the proportionality constant in Fick's first law for A diffusing through B; it is the flux per unit concentration gradient. SI unit: m²/s.

quiz.q: Why is D_AB = D_BA for a binary gas pair?
quiz.a: In a binary gas the same molecular motion carries A through B and B through A; swapping labels does not change the collision process. The symmetric Maxwell–Stefan coefficient gives D_AB = D_BA.

quiz.q: Use Fuller to estimate D for O2 in N2 at 350 K and 2 atm. Data: M_O2 = 32, M_N2 = 28, Σv O2 = 16.6, Σv N2 = 17.9.
A student measures D for CO2 in air with a two-bulb cell but forgets to thermostat; room temperature rises 5 K during the run. Will the reported D be too high or too low? Use T<sup>1.75</sup>.
quiz.a: D rises with T<sup>1.75</sup>, so the fitted slope is an average over a higher temperature. The reported D is too high compared with the value at the starting temperature; the run should be reported with its temperature range.

quiz.q: Why does the diaphragm cell need calibration with a known D?
quiz.a: The cell constant β contains the diaphragm's porosity and tortuosity, which are not known from its external dimensions. Calibrating with a pair of known D fixes β once for that cell.

quiz.q: Compare Stokes–Einstein and Fuller: which variables appear in each, and why does D depend on pressure for a gas but not explicitly for a liquid?
quiz.a: Stokes–Einstein has T, μ and r; Fuller has T, P, M and Σv. Gas D depends on P because pressure changes gas density and collision frequency. Liquid D depends strongly on viscosity, which changes mainly with T; pressure effects are small.

quiz.q: A liquid has viscosity 1.0 cP at 300 K. Estimate D for a solute of radius 0.5 nm using Stokes–Einstein. k_B = 1.381×10⁻²³ J/K.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern labs measure D by Taylor dispersion, pulsed-field gradient NMR and microfluidic tracking of single particles. Process simulators carry databases such as DIPPR and use group-contribution methods when data are missing. Research on ionic liquids, deep eutectic solvents and membranes needs D at high pressure and high temperature, where simple correlations fail. Search for 'Taylor dispersion analysis', 'pulsed-field gradient NMR diffusometry' and 'DIPPR diffusivity correlation'.
